title: The Sermon at Benares
subject: English

notes.heading: Word Meanings
points: Sermon: A religious or moral talk given by a spiritual leader.
Benares: The ancient holy city along the banks of the river Ganges, now known as Varanasi.
Enlightenment: A state of high spiritual knowledge, truth, and absolute awakening.
Scholarly: Relating to serious study, deep learning, and academic knowledge.
Chanced upon: Met or came across something completely by accident.
Alms: Money, clothes, or food given generously to poor people.
Renounce: To formally give up a claim, position, or way of life.
Afflicted: Suffering from severe physical pain, mental distress, or grief.
Preach: To deliver a religious sermon or give moral advice to a group.
Inscrutable: Something that is impossible to understand, interpret, or figure out.
Lamentation: An passionate expression of deep grief, sorrow, or weeping.
Slaughter: The killing of animals for food or the brutal killing of people.
Mortals: Living beings (especially humans) who are bound to die eventually.
Ripe: Fully grown, developed, and ready to fall or be collected.
Vessel: A hollow container, like a bowl or a pot, used to hold liquids.
Grief: Deep, intense mental sorrow caused by someone's death.
Weep: To shed tears or cry out of deep sadness.
Peace of mind: A mental state of calmness, quiet, and freedom from worry.

summary: "The Sermon at Benares" provides a profound insight into the early spiritual journey of Gautama Buddha and illuminates his core teaching regarding the inevitability of death and the universality of human suffering. Born a prince named Siddhartha Gautama in northern India, he lived a sheltered royal life until the age of twenty-five, when he chanced upon a sick man, an old man, a funeral procession, and a monk begging for alms. Deeply moved by this sudden exposure to the world's pervasive suffering, he renounced his crown, palace, and family to seek enlightenment regarding these human sorrows. After seven years of wandering, he attained spiritual awakening under a fig tree—which he renamed the Bodhi Tree (Tree of Wisdom)—and subsequently delivered his very first sermon at the holy city of Benares on the banks of the River Ganges. This sermon is beautifully illustrated through the story of a grieving woman named Kisa Gotami, whose only son had died. Overwhelmed by sorrow, she moved from neighbor to neighbor begging for a medicine to revive her child, leading a sympathetic man to direct her to the Buddha. The Buddha agreed to heal her son on one unique condition: she must bring him a handful of mustard seeds from a house where no child, husband, parent, or friend had ever died. Filled with hope, Kisa Gotami went from house to house, but everywhere she asked, she received the same tragic response—that the living were few, but the dead were many. Exhausted and hopeless, she sat by the wayside watching the city lights flicker and extinguish, a moment that sparked a profound realization: human lives are just like those lights,  flickering for a brief moment before being extinguished by death. Returning to the Buddha, she accepted that grief had made her selfish, understanding that death is the common destiny of all living beings. The Buddha then explained that the life of mortals in this world is troubled, brief, and combined with pain, emphasizing that just as ripe fruits are in danger of falling, or earthen vessels made by a potter are bound to break, all living things face the certainty of death. Ultimately, the sermon teaches that weeping and grieving will never restore the dead; instead, it only increases physical pain and damages the body, meaning that true peace of mind can only be achieved by overcoming sorrow, accepting the natural law of mortality, and drawing out the arrow of lamentation.

qa.q: What did Kisa Gotami ask for?
qa.a: ​ Kisa Gotami asked for medicine to bring her dead son back to life. She was unable to accept his death and went from house to house looking for help.

qa.q: Why did Kisa Gotami go from house to house?
qa.a: ​ Kisa Gotami went from house to house because she believed that someone might give her medicine to cure her dead son. A wise man finally directed her to the Buddha.

qa.q: What did the Buddha ask her to bring?
qa.a: ​ The Buddha asked Kisa Gotami to bring a handful of mustard seeds from a house where no one had ever died. He wanted her to understand that death is common to all families.

qa.q: What did Kisa Gotami understand when she returned to the Buddha?
qa.a: ​ Kisa Gotami understood that death is a natural and unavoidable part of life. She realised that no family is free from death and that she had to accept the loss of her son instead of remaining trapped in grief.

qa.q: How did the Buddha change Kisa Gotami’s understanding of life and death?
qa.a: ​ The Buddha helped Kisa Gotami understand that all living beings must eventually die. By asking her to find mustard seeds from a house untouched by death, he made her realise that suffering and death are common to everyone.

qa.q: What is the main message of the chapter?
qa.a: ​ The chapter teaches us that death is unavoidable and that we should accept it as a natural part of life. Excessive attachment to the dead causes suffering, while understanding the truth about life and death helps us find peace.

qa.q: Why was Kisa Gotami unable to accept her son’s death at first?
qa.a: ​ Kisa Gotami was deeply attached to her only son, so his death was unbearable for her. She was overwhelmed by grief and believed that he could somehow be brought back to life.
